problems.statement: About 1100 B.C., Chinese astronomers measured the maximum height of the Sun on the days of summer and winter solstices. In the former case, they obtained the value $h_1=79^\circ07'$, in the latter case $h_2=31^\circ19'$. On both the occasions, the Sun was south of zenith. Find out at what latitude the observations were made. Also calculate the angle between the ecliptic and the celestial equator in the epoch mentioned.

solution.statement:
The latitude may be found by formula:

$$\varphi=90^\circ-\frac{h_1+h_2}{2}=34^\circ47'.$$

The angle between the ecliptic and the celestial equator in the epoch mentioned:

$$\varepsilon=\frac{h_1-h_2}{2}=23^\circ54'.$$

problems.statement: The “Iridium” satellites give brilliant flares due to reflection of sunlight from their highly polished main mission antennas which are highly reflective plates, each of size $188\times86$ cm. A satellite was overhead at the time of the flare and the apparent magnitude of the flare was $-8^m$ at the centre.

solution.statement:
The drawing enables to realise that the light from the satellite actually spreads in a cone with angle $\alpha=0.5^\circ$, so that it covers area on the ground

$$S_E=\pi(\alpha h/2)^2.$$

Using the relation $m_1-m_2=-2.5\log(b_1/b_2)$ and taking into account stellar magnitude of the Sun $m_1=-26.8^m$ and magnitude of the flare $m_2=-8^m$, we can find that $(b_1/b_2)\approx3.3\cdot10^7$, and so we see $1/(3.3\cdot10^7)$ part of the Sun through the reflecting plate.

It means that the visible projection of the square of the plate $188\times86$ cm ($S=1.62$ m²) is $1/(3.3\cdot10^7)$ part of $\pi(\alpha h/2)^2$. Projection gives some factor about $2^{1/2}$ which should be taken into account since as usual we see the plate under the angle of $45^\circ$ (see figure):

$$S=\frac{2^{1/2}\pi(\alpha h/2)^2}{3.3\cdot10^7}.$$

Taking into account that $\alpha=9.1\cdot10^{-3}$ rad, one can find that $h\approx750$ km and the area on ground covered by the beams from one antenna

$$S_E=\pi(\alpha h/2)^2\approx40\ \mathrm{km}^2.$$

parts.label: a)
parts.statement: Draw a ray diagram and make a rough estimate of the area on ground covered by the beams from any one of the antennas.

parts.label: b)
parts.statement: Find the height of the satellite above the surface of the earth.

problems.statement:
We have received a message from Extraterrestrial Intelligence. Please decode it. The message is:

`10001100010011001001001001100111100100110010010010011001001000110`

(This is the whole message, not part of it.)

solution.statement:
There are 65 signs in the message. Having presented it as the table $5\times13$ (the alternative versions are not possible), we receive two possible solutions:

**5 columns, 13 lines**

```text
10001
10001
00110
01001
00100
11001
11100
10011
00100
10010
01100
10010
00110
```

**13 columns, 5 lines**

```text
1000110001001
1001001001001
1001111001001
1001001001001
1001001000110
```

After replacement of units on signs, and zero on gaps, the second version yields the quite understandable message:

![](p3-message)

“International Astronomical Union” or “1 astronomical unit”.

figures.alt: Original dot-pattern message: IAU or 1 AU.

problems.statement:
In the figure, you can see the intensity of radio emission (wavelength is about 21 cm) versus coordinate. Observational data has been obtained with a radio telescope and reduced. All interferences from atmosphere and receivers have been removed. One can measure several parameters from this profile. Please, state (without defining exactly the types of the parameters) how many parameters of this radio source can be measured in this record. Please, indicate these values in the figure.

A small optical telescope has been used to study this object. It was discovered that the fluxes in the radio and optical frequencies were equal. Which photons' number is more, radio or optical? By how many times is it more?

![](p4-radio)

solution.statement:
The profile is a curve combining 5 lines. Each line is a Gaussian characterized by 3 parameters: position of maximum on the horizontal axis, amplitude (height over zero) and half maximum width, describing its size. There are 5 lines in the Figure. It gives 5 parameters, and 1 additional parameter is a number of Gaussians. So 16 parameters.

Energy of each photon equals to $h\nu=hc/\lambda$. Therefore, for equal flux of energy, we observe more photons with lower energy, i.e. lower frequency (or longer wavelength $\lambda=21$ cm), than photons of visible light ($\lambda\sim550$ nm) approximately in 380 000 times ≈400 thousand times. Corresponding ration of numbers of photons is larger in the same times.

Answers: 16 parameters, number of radio photons is larger in 400 thousand times.

problems.statement: Estimate the orbital speed $V_G$ of Mars during Great oppositions with Earth. The orbital speed of Earth is $V_1=29.8$ km/s. The eccentricities of the orbits of the Earth and Mars are $e_1=0.017$ and $e_2=0.093$ respectively and the mean distance from the Sun to Mars is equal to $a_2=1.524$ a.u.

solution.statement:
Using the III Kepler law ($T^2/a^3=\mathrm{const}$) one can find that for the circular speed the following relation is valid:

$$V^2\cdot a=\mathrm{const}$$

and so:

$$V_{\mathrm{circ}}\sim a^{-1/2}$$

It means that the circular speed ($V_2$) for Mars orbit is $1.52^{1/2}$ smaller than one ($V_1$) for Earth orbit.

During the Great oppositions Mars is near the perihelion of its orbit.

Using the II Kepler law one may also write (for the orbits with small eccentricities – see note*):

$$V_{\mathrm{per}}\cdot R_{\mathrm{per}}=V_{\mathrm{circ}}\cdot R_{\mathrm{circ}}.$$
$$V_{\mathrm{per}}\cdot R_{\mathrm{circ}}(1-e)=V_{\mathrm{circ}}\cdot R_{\mathrm{circ}},$$

where $R_{\mathrm{circ}}$ and $V_{\mathrm{circ}}$ – the mean distance from the Sun to Mars and its mean orbital speed. So

$$V_G=V_{\mathrm{per}}=V_{\mathrm{circ}}/(1-e)=V_1/\{1.52^{1/2}(1-e)\}\approx26.6\ \mathrm{km/s}.$$

(*) More accurate using of the II Kepler law here is

$$V_{\mathrm{per}}\cdot a(1-e)/2=\pi ab/T,$$

where $a$ and $b$ are the semiaxes of the orbit, $b=a(1-e^2)^{1/2}$.

In this case the answer is

$$V_G=V_{\mathrm{circ}}\cdot\{(1+e)/(1-e)\}^{1/2}=V_1\cdot\{(1+e)/1.52(1-e)\}^{1/2}\approx26.5\ \mathrm{km/s}.$$

problems.statement: By a medium-size telescope, it is possible to detect an asteroid from the main asteroid belt down to a size of 5 km. Down to what size can objects of the Kuiper belt be registered by the same telescope using the same methods? You should remember by heart all the necessary properties and data of asteroids of the main belt and Kuiper belt. Consider the physical composition of the objects similar to Mars and Pluto respectively.

solution.statement:
The same intensity of light should be registered by the telescope form the asteroid of the main asteroid belt with size $D=5$ km and unknown yet asteroid of the Kuiper belt. The following aspects should be taken into account:

1. R. Distance from the Sun: 2.8 a.u. for the asteroid of the main belt and about 40 a.u. for the asteroid of the Kuiper belt. The intensity of light coming to the asteroids is reverse proportional to the square of these distances.
2. D. Size (diameter) of the body. The intensity of light reflecting by the body is proportional to the square of these sizes.
3. $\alpha$. Albedo. Albedo of Mars is about 0.15 and one of Pluto is 0.65. The intensity of light reflecting by the body is proportional to the albedos.
4. L. Distance from the observer (i.e. from the Earth): 1.8 a.u. for the asteroid of the main belt (in opposition) and about 40 a.u. for asteroid of Kuiper belt. The intensity of light coming to the telescope is reverse proportional to the square of these distances.

So $I\sim R^{-2}\cdot D^2\cdot\alpha\cdot L^{-2}$. And for $I_1=I_2$ we have to write:

$$D_2/D_1=(R_2/R_1)\cdot(L_2/L_1)\cdot(\alpha_1/\alpha_2)^{1/2}$$
$$D_2=5\ \mathrm{km}\cdot14\cdot22\cdot(0.23)^{1/2}\approx750\ \mathrm{km}.$$
